name: PT Lautan Luas Tbk

frontmatter.title: Lautan Luas: the market is paying for the trough, not for the earnings
frontmatter.summary: We initiate on Lautan Luas with a BUY rating and a Rp2,313 target, 178.5% total return. The market pays 8.3x trailing earnings and 0.4x book for a business that has just printed record nine-month revenue and an operating margin nearly double last year's [S2][S6]. Three things shape the call: the earnings reset, the through-cycle cash flow, and the liquidity and control discount we apply. The balance-sheet holdings are downside support, not bridge items [S6][S7].
thesis: The nine months to September 2026 are not a normalisation story: revenue reached IDR8,200.8bn and operating income IDR558.8bn, with the gross margin at 18.5% against 15.7% for the whole of FY2025, on both higher volumes and better selling prices [S2][S6].
Our primary DCF values the share at Rp2,496; the probability-weighted, liquidity-adjusted twelve-month value is Rp2,313, and the base scenario alone is worth Rp2,626 [S0].

The through-cycle DCF carries the value at 75% of the blend. The peer EV/EBITDA leg at 15% is applied to the data pack's FY2025 trailing EBITDA — the trough year — so it is a floor, not the value; the dividend-capacity leg at 10% applies the sector yield to the forward payout; a P/E on the same trough profit would measure the impairments and the minority mix rather than the cycle, so it carries no weight [S0][S5].

The balance sheet is downside support, not a bridge item: associates at IDR653.3bn enter the bridge only net of the present value of their modelled losses, while equity instruments at IDR353.7bn and investment properties at IDR452.3bn are excluded from value because their income already sits in the earnings we capitalise; parent equity is IDR3,461.7bn [S6].

What tempers the call is liquidity and control: PT Caturkarsa Megatunggal holds 56.6% and the public 36.1%, with treasury stock at 6.1%, and three-month average daily value traded is IDR203.0m, so the engine strips 20.0% from the weighted value before setting the target [S10][S0].
The risk that matters is a faster reversal of chemical and plastics prices than the Brent deck assumes, with import competition already visible in the industry association's complaints [S12].

catalysts.event: Maturity of the series B bond due in November 2026 — the first half of the refinancing test; the company says it has scheduled the payment, so the test is the price and tenor of the replacement [S9][S2]
FY2026 audited accounts and annual report — the first full year carrying the restated depreciation base and the nine-month margin gains [S5]
Maturity of the 2024 series bonds in July 2027 — the second refinancing test [S5]
Gross margin and working capital cycle: the two lines that decide whether the nine-month gain holds [S2][S7]

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Lautan Luas Tbk with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp2,313, against a price of Rp850 on the last close we hold. Including the dividend we expect over the period, Rp54 a share, the expected total return is 178.5% [S0].

The market is valuing a business that earned IDR149.5bn for its owners in FY2025 at 8.3x those earnings and 0.4x parent book value, even though the first nine months of 2026 have already produced IDR195.6bn of attributable profit and an operating margin that nearly doubled year on year [S2][S6]. We do not think the market is missing the results; the shares trade at Rp850 against a fifty-two-week high of Rp1,075 [S0]. What the price is doing, in our reading, is refusing to capitalise a cyclical margin at anything like a normal multiple for a company with a thin free float, a controlling shareholder and a bond wall to refinance [S5][S7].

Three things shape the call. The first is the earnings reset: revenue of IDR8,200.8bn in the nine months to September 2026 is 27.6% higher than a year earlier, operating income reached IDR558.8bn against IDR412.7bn for the whole of FY2025, and the gross margin of 18.5% came with a working capital cycle of 52.0 days rather than a build [S2][S6]. The second is the balance sheet, which is downside support rather than a source of value in the target: associates carried at IDR653.3bn enter the bridge only net of the present value of the losses they are forecast to absorb, and we exclude the equity instruments of IDR353.7bn and the investment properties of IDR452.3bn from value altogether, because the income they generate already sits inside the earnings we capitalise and adding their book again would double count [S6]. The third is what we deliberately give back: because the shares are illiquid, the engine takes 20.0% off the probability-weighted value before the target is set, which is why the target is Rp2,313 rather than the Rp2,891 the scenarios average to [S0].

Our primary method is a ten-year discounted cash flow at a weighted average cost of capital of 12.4%, and it produces Rp2,496. It carries 75% of the blend. The peer-median EV/EBITDA method at 15% gives Rp1,218: it sits -51.2% below the DCF because the engine can only read the data pack's last-twelve-months series, which falls back to FY2025 — the trough year, with EBITDA of IDR559.2bn on a 15.7% gross margin [S0][S5]. We keep that leg as the floor value if the trough, not FY2026E, is the normal year. The dividend-capacity leg at 10% gives Rp2,053 on the forward payout, the anchor the market is actually using. A P/E applied to the same trough profit would capitalise the impairments booked above the operating line and the minority mix, so it is set to zero weight rather than carried [S5][S6]. The valuation section works through the basis effect rather than hiding it.

What would make us wrong is not a bad quarter but a bad cycle. The industry association says petrochemical and plastics producers are under pressure from cheaper imports and is asking the ministry for safeguard and anti-dumping measures [S12]. If chemical prices roll over faster than the Brent deck assumes, the nine-month margin compresses toward the FY2025 trough, and our bear case of Rp1,043 is the honest marker of that path.

PT Lautan Luas is an integrated ingredients and solutions provider that began as an importer of basic and specialty chemicals and now runs three segments: distribution, manufacturing, and support and services [S7]. Distribution takes chemical products from international principals and delivers them to Indonesian industry; manufacturing makes specialty chemicals and ingredients, including water-treatment chemicals; and the support and services segment sells technical services, warehousing and water-treatment solutions around the products [S7][S10].

The segment mix is the key to the economics. In FY2025 distribution produced external revenue of IDR4,513.9bn, manufacturing IDR3,695.8bn and support and services IDR589.4bn. The profit pool is weighted differently: distribution earned segment gross profit of IDR617.7bn, manufacturing IDR699.6bn and services IDR124.7bn [S5]. Manufacturing therefore converts a smaller revenue base into a larger gross profit than distribution, and services, though small, earns the widest margin of the three. By the first nine months of 2026 the mix had shifted slightly toward manufacturing: distribution remained the largest line by revenue, manufacturing the second and services a small remainder [S2].

The distribution business is the scale engine. It is supported by more than a hundred international principals and over a thousand products, spread across Indonesia, Singapore, Shanghai, Thailand and Vietnam, and serves food and beverages, animal feed, water, personal care, agriculture, mining, plastics and rubber [S7]. In Indonesia it operates through four branches, five representative offices and one bonded warehouse [S2]. That footprint is the asset: a principal that wants national coverage of a thousand product lines in a market with fragmented regional distributors is buying reach, bonded inventory and technical support, not just a purchase order.

Manufacturing is where the capital and the margin sit. The group runs seven manufacturing subsidiaries and four support and services subsidiaries [S2]. The water-treatment franchise is the strategic piece: the partnership with Organo Corporation of Japan dates from 2013, and in April 2025 the company raised its ownership of PT Lautan Organo Water from a minority position to a controlling majority, taking control and consolidating it [S10]. That transaction explains part of the year-on-year step in revenue and in minority interest, and it is why the water and chemicals businesses are named as the growth drivers in the 2026 plan [S2][S10]. Its arithmetic is small: the support and services segment where LOW sits was 6.7% of FY2025 revenue and grew 13.5% that year, so even if the whole of that segment's growth were the consolidation it would add only a fraction of a percentage point to the 27.6% nine-month revenue growth [S10][S2]. The step is therefore organic — volume and price — not a consolidation artefact, and the FY2027E growth rate in our model is struck off a base that already contains a full year of LOW.

The company's own plan for 2026, set at the end of 2025, targeted revenue growth of 7.0% to 9.0% and an attributable net margin of 1.5% to 3.0% of revenue, with net interest-bearing debt to equity projected at about 0.4x — the last of these a capital-structure target rather than a forecast [S10]. The first nine months have already beaten the revenue target, which tells us the plan underestimated the price effect in chemicals rather than that management is sandbagging.

Control is concentrated. PT Caturkarsa Megatunggal is both the immediate parent and the ultimate parent of the group and holds 56.6% of the shares; two directors, Pranata Hajadi and Indrawan Masrin, hold 0.6% and 0.6%; treasury stock is 6.1%; and the public holds 36.1% [S10]. The company employs 3,143 people [S0]. We treat the controlling shareholder as permanent, not as a seller, and value the minority stake accordingly.

Chemical distribution in Indonesia is a relationship and logistics business before it is a manufacturing business. The distributor's edge comes from holding exclusive or semi-exclusive principal mandates, from carrying the working capital that lets it hold stock in bonded warehouses, and from technical service that helps customers reformulate. Manufacturing of specialty chemicals and water-treatment chemistry sits on top of that network, earns a wider margin and consumes more capital. Global majors have generally chosen to reach Indonesian industry through local partners rather than build their own distribution, which is the structural reason a company of this kind can earn a return above its cost of capital through a cycle even when commodity chemical prices are falling.

The demand backdrop improved through 2026. The chemicals, pharmaceuticals and traditional medicine industry grew 8.1% in the third quarter of 2026, according to the government's growth briefing, driven by the completion of chemical-sector investments and by pharmaceutical expansion to supply the national health programme [S11]. That matters for Lautan Luas because its distribution book sells into exactly those chains: food ingredients, personal and home care, water treatment, and basic and specialty chemicals are the four drivers the company names for 2026 [S10].

The same industry is under import pressure. The plastics and petrochemical association says producers are being squeezed by cheaper imported product and has asked the Ministry of Industry for safeguard and anti-dumping measures, while the minister has promised protection through standards and trade remedies [S12]. This cuts both ways for a distributor. Cheaper imports lower the price of what it sells, which compresses revenue per tonne and can force inventory write-downs; but a distributor with principal relationships and technical service earns a margin on the service and the bundle, and is less exposed to the domestic producer's cost position than a manufacturer would be. The risk is real in the commodity end of the range, where price is the only differentiator.

The demand drivers are worth separating. Water treatment is the most structural: Indonesian industrial and municipal water infrastructure is under-built, and the group's Organo partnership puts it inside the technical specification of new plants rather than at the commodity end of the market [S10]. Food ingredients and personal care are volume businesses with reformulation service attached, where a distributor's application laboratory is the differentiator [S7][S10]. Agriculture and mining are cyclical and price-sensitive. Plastics and rubber are the most exposed to import competition and to the oil price [S12].

On competitive position, we would characterise Lautan Luas as the scale incumbent in Indonesian chemical distribution rather than a price-setter. Its advantages are the breadth of principal relationships, the product range, the national logistics footprint and the bonded warehouse, and the technical service capability in water and food [S7][S2]. Its disadvantages are that it does not own the brands it distributes, that principals can and do appoint second distributors, and that its customers are large industrial buyers with purchasing power. The result is a business that earns a distribution margin in the low teens on the traded book and a manufacturing margin in the high teens on its own products, with returns that depend on volume and working capital discipline rather than on pricing power [S5].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high and rising: the principals own the product and the brand, and the distributor's switching cost runs the other way. Buyer power is moderate to high in food and personal care, where customers are large and can multi-source, and lower in water treatment, where the specification and service relationship bind. The threat of new entrants is moderate in distribution, because working capital and principal relationships are barriers, and low in water-treatment chemistry, where process know-how and the Organo relationship matter. Substitutes are a slow force: formulators can change a chemical input, but the service bundle usually survives the substitution. Rivalry is intense in commodity chemicals and moderate in specialty [S5][S12].

The macro deck sets the frame for costs. The rupiah is at Rp18,103/USD against the dollar at the time of writing, while the deck's average for FY2026E is Rp17,570/USD, so imported chemical costs are translating at a weaker rate than the year's average, and Brent is put at US$96.0/bbl for FY2026E, falling through the deck's explicit years to US$78.0/bbl by FY2029 and a little lower again in FY2030 and then escalating again toward the mid-eighties by FY2035, above the deck's long-run marker of US$75.0/bbl [d.macro][d.oil.brent]. A distributor passes most of that through with a lag; what it cannot pass through is the working capital cost of carrying inventory whose replacement cost is falling [S7][S5].

The structural feature of this industry is that the distributor's return on capital is driven by inventory turns and receivable days, not by gross margin alone. A percentage point of gross margin is worth less than a week of working capital cycle when volumes are growing, because the funding cost of receivables and stock is carried on the distributor's balance sheet while the principal keeps the brand. That is why the companies that survive cycles are the ones with the widest principal mandates and the tightest credit control, and why the market watches working capital days as closely as the margin.

The first thing to fix in the historical data is depreciation. The data pack originally carried FY2025 D&A at roughly a third of the audited figure. The accounts allocate IDR146.6bn of fixed-asset depreciation across cost of goods sold, services, selling and general expenses, so we restate the line from the notes for FY2024 and FY2025; that is why FY2025 D&A in our model is IDR146.6bn and FY2024 EBITDA is IDR571.0bn rather than the pack's lower numbers [S5]. Right-of-use depreciation of IDR50.2bn and intangible amortisation of IDR0.5bn are disclosed separately and excluded from the engine line so that the cash-flow add-back matches the fixed-asset roll-forward [S5].

FY2025 was a trough year on the income statement. Revenue of IDR8,799.2bn produced a gross margin of 15.7%, EBITDA of IDR559.2bn and attributable profit of IDR149.5bn, or Rp102 a share on the current share count [S5]. The margin was squeezed because cost of goods sold grew faster than revenue, and the operating result was held up by other operating income of IDR94.3bn against other operating expenses of IDR68.2bn — a net contribution that is the gap between gross profit less operating expenses and the reported operating income [S5]. We show the reported operating income of IDR412.7bn in the model and calibrate the opex ratio so that forecasts are struck on the same basis.

The first nine months of 2026 changed the picture. Revenue of IDR8,200.8bn generated gross profit of IDR1,516.4bn, operating income of IDR558.8bn and attributable profit of IDR195.6bn, with company-reported EBITDA of IDR665.0bn [S6][S2]. The gross margin of 18.5% is nearly three percentage points above the FY2025 level, and operating expenses grew far more slowly than revenue, so the operating margin expanded from both ends [S2][S6]. This is the one calibration gap in the model worth naming: our FY2026E EBITDA margin of 8.0% sits above the FY2025 audited 6.4% because it is built on the nine-month actual of IDR665.0bn on IDR8,200.8bn rather than on the trough year; holding the forecast at the FY2025 margin would contradict the filing. Part of the operating expense line in the nine months is one-off: other operating expenses of IDR68.2bn in FY2025 became a much larger charge in the nine months of 2026 after impairments of an associate, of other receivables and of amounts due from related parties, which is why our FY2026E operating expense ratio of 11.5% is above the 11.1% we hold thereafter [S6].

Our forecast builds revenue of IDR10,801.0bn for FY2026E, growing 22.8%, then IDR11,233.0bn and IDR11,794.7bn as growth settles to 4.0% and 5.0% [S0][d.oil.brent]. The deceleration is deliberate and comes from the oil deck: Brent of US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E falls to US$84.0/bbl and to US$78.0/bbl by FY2029, with its low in FY2030, and because a distributor's revenue is largely the price of the product it moves, a falling oil price pulls nominal revenue growth down even as volumes grow [d.oil.brent][S10]. From FY2030 the deck turns up again, so the model holds nominal growth at the terminal rate rather than claiming a further oil-driven deceleration; the margin, not the top line, is where the outer years do their work. The gross margin is modelled at base input costs with a Brent link: we treat 40.0% of cost of goods sold as oil-exposed and 95.0% of any move as passed through in price, so the net margin sensitivity is small [S5][d.oil.brent]. After the link, the effective margin is 17.9% in FY2026E and 17.6% in FY2027E, settling near the four-year mean rather than at the 2026 peak [S5][S7].

The earnings path follows: EBIT of IDR691.6bn, IDR727.6bn and IDR723.2bn, EBITDA of IDR859.0bn in FY2026E, attributable profit of IDR263.8bn and earnings per share of Rp180, rising to Rp193 [S0]. Dividends at a 30.0% payout are Rp54 for FY2026E against Rp31 paid for FY2025 [S5, S7]. Minority interests are forecast at 29.2% of net profit, the nine-month 2026 actual rather than the FY2025 trough-year share, because the manufacturing subsidiaries where the minorities sit are now the profit engine and nothing in the filing shows that mix reversing [S5][S6].

Cash conversion is the weak spot. FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR128.7bn against capital expenditure of IDR215.3bn and a working capital build that took operating working capital from IDR756.3bn to IDR1,139.1bn, so free cash flow to the firm was negative [S5]. The nine months of 2026 repeated the pattern in the balance sheet even as the working capital cycle improved: receivables of IDR1,804.6bn, inventories of IDR1,509.5bn and payables of IDR1,668.7bn plus IDR23.5bn to related parties [S6]. Our model assumes operating working capital at 14.2% of revenue, consistent with the 52.0 days cycle, which means FY2026E absorbs another working capital outflow before the cash flow normalises [S2].

The balance sheet is where the risk concentrates. At the end of September 2026 the company had interest-bearing debt of Rp1,523bn and cash of IDR354.8bn, net debt to EBITDA of 1.3x, and a current ratio of 1.1x [S6][S7][S2]. Within the current stack sit short-term bank loans of IDR860.4bn and bonds of IDR419.2bn classified as current, against current assets of IDR4,136.2bn and current liabilities of IDR3,586.5bn [S6]. The bonds themselves are unsecured: Rp135bn of series B notes mature in November 2026 and Rp286bn of the 2024 series in July 2027 [S5]. The company says it has scheduled the payment of the November maturity, and the improvement in net debt to EBITDA to 1.3x over the year shows the operating cash is there; the question is the price and tenor of the refinancing, not the ability to pay [S9][S2].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly but modest. Dividends paid were IDR65.9bn in FY2025 and IDR52.0bn in FY2024, a payout at the 30.0% level the model holds, and the buyback programme that ran from September 2023 to February 2025 repurchased 90.2m shares at an average price well above today's Rp850 [S10][S5]. With capital expenditure at 1.8% of revenue there is no large project absorbing the cash, so the choice is between debt reduction, a higher dividend and acquisitions; the model assumes debt held flat and lets cash accumulate, which is the neutral assumption rather than a prediction [S10].

On earnings quality we flag four things. First, cash conversion: profit has run ahead of operating cash flow for two years because working capital grows with revenue, which is normal for a distributor but leaves no cushion if growth stops [S5]. Second, the associate book: the share of losses was IDR44.3bn in FY2025 and IDR52.4bn in the nine months of 2026, and the company impaired an associate in both periods, so the IDR653.3bn carrying value is not a certain asset [S5][S6]. Third, the minority share of profit jumped from a low base in FY2025 to a much higher share in the nine months of 2026, which reduces the value of each rupiah of group profit to the parent's holders [S5][S6]. Fourth, the non-operating lines are volatile — gains on asset sales, dividend income, impairments of receivables and of related-party balances — and we have normalised rather than extrapolated them [S5][S6].

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method because the value of this business is the cash it generates after the working capital it must fund, and because a distributor's earnings multiple is a poor guide when the margin is at a cyclical peak or trough. The cost of capital build follows the engine exactly: it starts from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, deducts the Indonesian default spread of 1.6% that the macro deck carries, adds a levered beta of 1.76 multiplied by the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, and then adds the 1.0% illiquidity premium [S0][d.macro]. The beta is the industry unlevered beta of 0.90 relevered at a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.22, which is high because the market capitalisation is small against the debt stack [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 18.6%. Debt costs 9.4% before tax, and at weights of 45.0% equity and 55.0% debt the weighted average cost of capital is 12.4%.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR4,901.4bn and an equity value of Rp2,496 a share. The terminal value is 47.1% of enterprise value, which is high but not extreme for a ten-year horizon; the first explicit year contributes little because FY2026E absorbs a working capital build of roughly the size of the year's free cash flow [S0]. The bridge from enterprise to equity uses the 30 September 2026 balance sheet restated from the filing: it subtracts net debt of IDR1,523.0bn of interest-bearing debt less IDR354.8bn of cash, subtracts non-controlling interest of IDR314.6bn, and adds the associates at their carrying value of IDR653.3bn less the present value of the loss stream the base case carries for them. The arithmetic is worth setting out, because it is the one place where the operating model and the bridge interact. The associates' losses sit below the operating line at -70bn a year in every forecast year and are therefore excluded from the free cash flow the DCF discounts, so an associate added at book would be counted as an asset while the cost of owning it is left out of the value. Discounting that same annual loss on the engine's own schedule — the remaining part of FY2026E at a factor of one, then each of FY2027E to FY2035E at the discount factor the engine applies to that year's cash flow, all at the 12.4% weighted average cost of capital — gives a present value that is deducted from the IDR653.3bn carrying value, and the deduction is the bridge item carried in the model, line by line, in the assumptions record. What remains for the associates is a fraction of book rather than book itself [S6]. We do not extrapolate the loss beyond the explicit horizon, because the flat run-rate is a modelling convention rather than a claim that the associates lose money in perpetuity, and we do not stack a second book haircut on top: the loss stream is precisely why the book has already been impaired twice, so deducting both would count the same concern twice [S6][F66]. We do not add the equity instruments of IDR353.7bn or the investment properties of IDR452.3bn separately, because the income they generate sits inside other operating income and is therefore already in the earnings we capitalise; adding their book value as well would double count [S6].

We apply three methods, and say what each is for. The DCF is the value: Rp2,496 at 75% of the blend, because it is the only instrument that capitalises the whole cycle rather than one year of it. The EV/EBITDA method is the floor: Rp1,218 at 15%, on a peer median of 5.4x applied to the data pack's last-twelve-months EBITDA, which falls back to FY2025 — the trough year, IDR559.2bn — through the same September bridge [S0][S5]. It sits -51.2% below the DCF, and that gap is the cycle rather than a disagreement about the business. The dividend-capacity leg is the market's own anchor: Rp2,053 at 10%, the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp54 capitalised at the peer median yield of 2.6%, which sits -17.7% below the DCF and is the basis on which the shares actually trade [S0].

Why we do not simply pin both legs to FY2026E earnings. The peer multiples the engine holds are trailing multiples of the peers' own last reported year [S0]. Pairing a trailing peer multiple with our forward earnings would value next year's profit on the peers' current rating, which is the procyclical error the industry method card bans; the internally consistent pairing is trailing with trailing, and the through-cycle job belongs to the DCF. On our FY2026E EBITDA the same peer median produces a value well above the trough-basis floor and much closer to the DCF — which is what we would expect, since FY2026E's margin is close to the four-year mean rather than to the trough — but we do not weight it, because it would be a trailing multiple on forward earnings [S0][S5]. The P/E leg is set to zero for the same reason plus one of its own: FY2025 attributable profit is distorted both by the trough margin and by the impairments booked inside other operating expenses above the operating line, and by a minority share that has since risen, so it measures neither the cycle nor the equity holder's claim on it [S5][S6]. The weighted value of the blend is Rp2,260.

The scenarios are mirrored around the base, driver for driver. The bear case cuts revenue growth enough to make FY2027E an outright decline, takes the gross margin down to the FY2025 trough of 15.7%, reprices the whole debt stack at a higher rate at the refinancing, and assumes a modest equity issue to fund working capital. The bull case adds the same revenue growth and the same margin, reprices the debt lower as the policy rate eases, and retires part of the register each year through a resumed buyback. The probabilities are 50.0% for the base and 25.0% for each tail, and the values run from Rp1,043 in the bear case through Rp2,626 in the base to Rp5,270 in the bull [S0]. The bull value is larger in percentage terms than the bear is smaller because a distributor's operating leverage is high once the margin recovers and the working capital cycle holds; that is the same leverage that makes the bear case uncomfortable, which is why we do not present the upper tail as the base.

The method card for this industry asks for a dividend-capacity anchor alongside the NAV, and the two point in different directions, which is the whole point. Our FY2026E dividend of Rp54 at a 30.0% payout is a yield of 6.4% at today's price and 6.8% on our FY2027E forecast. Capitalised at our DCF value, the same dividend is a yield roughly a third as large, so the market at Rp850 is valuing the share on its dividend stream, not on the cash flow the DCF sees: the dividend-capacity anchor is what the price is using, and the through-cycle NAV is what we use. That is why the dividend leg of the blend, at Rp2,053, sits below the DCF but well above the price. The gap is the re-rating we are underwriting, and it will not close until the leverage that sits between the two falls. Net debt of IDR1,523.0bn of interest-bearing debt less IDR354.8bn of cash is a little over twice the FY2025 trough EBITDA of IDR559.2bn — the number the bond market will look at when the November maturity is refinanced [S6][S5].

What the price implies is the most useful cross-check we have. At Rp850 the shares change hands at 4.7x our FY2026E earnings and 3.2x our FY2026E EBITDA, so the market is valuing the operating business at a little over half of the peer median EBITDA multiple on earnings it has already begun to deliver [S0][S6][S7]. The reverse DCF cannot bracket that price inside the engine's solve range, which is itself the answer: to get from our cash flows to today's price requires a discount rate far above the one the balance sheet and the beta support, or a permanent reversal in the margin. We think the market is applying a governance and liquidity discount larger than the 20.0% we apply, and we say so plainly rather than dress it up as a fundamental view [S0]. That discount is a house parameter set by the traded-value schedule, not state-dependent in our target construction: we take it off every scenario, including the bull, because the shares turn over IDR203.0m a day and a position cannot be built or exited at NAV. What would retire it is turnover rising through the house threshold, which depends on the register — 36.1% public and 6.1% treasury stock today — not on the earnings; until then the bull case expresses the re-rating through the earnings and the cost of capital, and the discount stands.

Finally, the target, step by step. The method blend gives Rp2,260 a share today. Rolled forward twelve months at the 18.6% cost of equity and net of the Rp54 of dividends expected over that period, the base case is Rp2,626. The three scenarios are then weighted 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull, at Rp1,043, Rp2,626 and Rp5,270, which gives Rp2,891. The engine applies a 20.0% discount for the illiquid register and the IDR203.0m of average daily turnover, which gives the Rp2,313 target, and the dividend of Rp54 takes the total return to 178.5% [S0]. That is the number behind the BUY rating. The dividend-capacity anchor — 6.4% on our FY2026E payout — is what makes the wait bearable while the re-rating closes.

The first risk is the cycle. The nine-month gross margin of 18.5% is well above the FY2025 trough of 15.7% and above the four-year average, and it was earned while chemical prices were rising [S2][S5]. A distributor earns inventory gains when prices rise and inventory losses when they fall; the same margin that expanded on the way up compresses on the way down, and the operating leverage that produced the earnings increase works in reverse. Our bear case takes the margin back to that trough and one year of falling revenue, and on those assumptions the value is Rp1,043, which is still above the current price, but the path to it would be uncomfortable [S0].

The second is import competition and trade policy. The plastics and petrochemical association says its members are under pressure from cheaper imports and has asked for safeguard and anti-dumping action, and the government has promised standards and trade remedies [S12]. For Lautan Luas the transmission is through the price of the commodity end of its range and through inventory values; a safeguard would help domestic producers but could raise the cost of imported product the distributor sells. The direction of policy is uncertain in both directions, which is why we treat it as a risk rather than a forecast.

The third is refinancing and liquidity. Short-term bank loans of IDR860.4bn and bonds of IDR419.2bn classified as current, against current assets of IDR4,136.2bn and current liabilities of IDR3,586.5bn, mean the company is relying on rolling bank lines and on the bond market at the same time [S6]. The Rp135bn maturity in November 2026 and the Rp286bn maturity in July 2027 are small against the asset base but large against the free cash flow of a working-capital-heavy year [S5]. If the refinancing is done at a materially higher rate than the coupons now in issue, the interest line rises and the equity value falls [S5]. The base case assumes refinancing in place at the 9.0% cost of debt the model carries; the bear case reprices the whole stack at a materially higher rate and cuts the value accordingly, which is where the risk is priced.

The fourth is the associate book. Associates carried at IDR653.3bn generated losses of IDR44.3bn in FY2025 and IDR52.4bn in the nine months of 2026, and the company impaired one of them in both periods [S5][S6]. If the losses continue, the carrying value is at risk and the equity bridge in our valuation overstates value by the amount of any further impairment. Our base case carries the associate loss at -70bn a year in every forecast year — the annualised nine-month run rate — because the impairment the company took in 2026 sits inside other operating expenses above the operating line and cannot offset the below-the-line share of losses [S6]. The bridge deducts the present value of that loss stream from the book value, so the value we carry for the associates is already net of the losses we forecast; what it does not carry is a write-off of the whole book, which would be worse than our bear.

The fifth is the minority leakage. Minorities took a much larger share of profit in the nine months of 2026 than in FY2025, because the manufacturing subsidiaries where they sit are the ones that recovered [S5][S6]. If manufacturing keeps outgrowing distribution, the parent's share of group profit grows more slowly than group profit, and the value per share is lower than a group-level model implies.

The sixth is governance and control. The controlling shareholder holds 56.6% and the public 36.1%, with 6.1% in treasury stock, which means the market for the shares is thin, the price can move on small flows, and a minority holder has limited influence [S10]. Related-party balances are small relative to the balance sheet — trade receivables from related parties of IDR10.0bn against IDR1,804.6bn from third parties — but the group structure is layered and the associates are related parties, so the risk is one of valuation rather than of outright expropriation [S6].

The seventh is currency. The rupiah is at Rp18,103/USD against the dollar, weaker than the FY2026E average in the macro deck of Rp17,570/USD, and the group imports a large share of what it distributes [d.macro][S7]. A weaker rupiah raises the cost of imported product and the working capital needed to carry it; pass-through is high but lagged, so a sharp move hits one or two quarters of margin.

The signposts we would watch are the quarterly gross margin, where a fall back toward the FY2025 level would confirm the cycle has turned; the working capital cycle, where a reversal from 52.0 days would signal that growth is being bought with credit; the terms of the bond refinancing; and any safeguard or anti-dumping decision [S2][S5][S12]. A quarter of stable margin at current volumes would keep us with the base case; two quarters of margin compression would push us toward the bear.

Ownership and control are concentrated and stable. PT Caturkarsa Megatunggal is the immediate parent and the ultimate parent of the group and holds 56.6% of the shares; the two directors on the register hold 0.6% and 0.6%, treasury stock is 6.1% and the public holds 36.1% [S10]. The public stake is thin enough that the engine's liquidity discount of 20.0% is a fair reflection of what a minority holder could realise, though the discount is set by the traded-value schedule rather than by the ownership percentages [S0]. There is no evidence of a change of control, a tender or a group restructuring in the period we cover.

On disclosure and audit, the FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, a member firm of the Ernst & Young global network, with an unqualified opinion [S5]. The annual report states that neither the company, its subsidiaries, nor any serving commissioner or director was involved in a civil or criminal case, an arbitration, a tax dispute or a bankruptcy or debt-suspension proceeding in 2025, and that no material administrative sanction was imposed [S10]. That is the clean end of the disclosure range for an Indonesian small cap.

Related-party dealings are modest on the face of the balance sheet. Trade receivables from related parties were IDR10.0bn at the end of September 2026 against IDR1,804.6bn from third parties, and trade payables to related parties IDR23.5bn against IDR1,668.7bn to third parties [S6]. The associate book of IDR653.3bn is the larger related-party exposure, because the associates are part of the group's water and chemicals network [S6]. The risk here is valuation rather than diversion: related-party sales and purchases are disclosed at arm's length and are small relative to the group.

The dividend record is steady but cyclical. Dividends per share were Rp50 for FY2022, Rp35 for FY2023, Rp45 for FY2024 and Rp31 for FY2025, so the payout moves with earnings rather than being fixed [S5][S7]. The buyback that ended in February 2025 repurchased 90.2m shares, a meaningful return of capital for a company of this size, at an average price above the current market [S10]. A company that buys its own shares above today's price is either confident in the cycle or was wrong about it; the subsequent earnings recovery suggests the former, but it also reduced the free float.

On ESG, the group's manufacturing subsidiaries carry the environmental exposure that a chemicals business carries: effluent, hazardous materials handling and energy use. The disclosed record is compliance rather than leadership. PT Lautan Luas received an EcoVadis sustainability assessment committed badge in October 2025, PT Dunia Kimia Jaya received the same badge in August 2025 and a gold Indonesia Responsible Care Award in October 2025, and the Semarang plant holds a blue, compliant rating under the environment ministry's corporate performance programme [S10]. There is no disclosed emissions target in the materials we hold, and the sustainability report is referenced rather than reproduced. For a distributor and specialty manufacturer the transition risk is moderate: the products themselves are not the source of a large direct carbon liability, but customers in food and personal care are beginning to ask for supply-chain emissions data, and the water-treatment business is a positive exposure to the transition rather than a negative one.

For a company of this kind the material governance questions are the ones that do not show up in a compliance statement: whether the controlling family treats the listed entity as the primary vehicle or as one asset among several, whether related-party transactions are priced at arm's length, and whether the board has the independence to challenge a related-party deal. The clean audit opinion and the small related-party balances answer the second question for now; the concentration of ownership answers the first, in the sense that minority holders are passengers rather than drivers.

The nearest dated catalyst is the November 2026 maturity of the Rp135bn series B bond. The company says it has scheduled the payment; the terms on which it refinances the bond, or replaces it with bank lines, will tell us what the market is charging for its credit [S5][S9]. The second is the July 2027 maturity of the Rp286bn 2024 series bonds, which is the larger test and the one that sets the interest cost in our forecast [S5].

The results calendar is the other set of dates. The FY2026 audited accounts and annual report, expected around April 2027, will be the first full-year set that carries the restated depreciation base and a full year of the nine-month margin gains, and they will show whether the fourth quarter held [S5][S7]. Before that, the quarterly trading updates give the margin and working capital cycle, which are the two lines that decide whether the base case or the bear case is right [S2].

On policy, any safeguard or anti-dumping decision affecting petrochemicals and plastics imports is a catalyst in both directions, and the industry association's lobbying makes a decision plausible within our horizon [S12]. On capital returns, the dividend for FY2026 will be proposed at the annual meeting in 2027, and the payout of 30.0% we assume is the level the company has held through the cycle [S5][S7].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the gross margin, the working capital cycle, the EBITDA to interest cover, the net debt to EBITDA ratio and the minority share of profit [S2][S7]. The first two tell us whether the cycle is holding; the last three tell us whether the balance sheet and the group structure are helping or hurting the equity holder.

bear.narrative: A full chemical and plastics down-cycle: cheaper imports force distributors to compete on price, revenue falls outright for a year, the gross margin returns to the FY2025 trough, the bond and bank lines reprice three hundred basis points higher, and a modest equity issue funds working capital while the associate losses continue.

bull.narrative: Water-treatment project wins and food-ingredient and personal-care volumes hold the high-teens gross margin into FY2027, revenue grows faster as the 2026 selling-price gains stick, the refinancing is done at a lower rate as the BI rate eases, and a resumed buyback retires two per cent of the register a year.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E marks up the nine-month actual: revenue of Rp8,200.8bn to September 2026 is 27.6% above the Rp6,424.9bn of the same period and already far beyond the 7%-9% growth the company planned for the year, because volumes and selling prices both rose [F26, S2, F44, F49]. A normal seasonal fourth quarter (FY2025's fourth quarter contributed Rp2,374.3bn of the Rp8,799.2bn year) taken at roughly ten percent year-on-year growth gives about Rp10.8tn for FY2026E, or 22.75% growth. From FY2027E the build decelerates to 4%, then 5%, 4.5% and 4%: the Brent deck falls from US$96 to US$84 and then US$75, which pulls nominal chemical prices down, so the growth left is the volume the company names as its 2026 drivers (food ingredients, personal home care, water treatment, basic and specialty chemicals) plus the water-treatment project pipeline [S10, d.oil.brent]. The terminal rate matches the long-run nominal growth of the reporting currency.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Set at base input costs, meaning FY2025A Brent of US$68.10, with the oil link applied on top. The path is anchored on what the accounts show: 15.7% in FY2025 (a trough), 17.5% in FY2024, 16.2% in FY2023 and 19.1% in FY2022, a four-year mean near 17.4%, and 18.5% in the nine months to September 2026 as volumes recovered and selling prices improved [S5, S7, F31]. FY2026E is set so that after the Brent link it lands on the 18.5% nine-month actual less a weaker fourth quarter (FY2025's fourth quarter gross margin was in the mid-teens); the outer years settle back toward the four-year mean as the oil deck normalises and the current price gains are competed away, not below it [d.oil.brent, S2].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Calibration, not a company disclosure: 40% of cost of goods sold is treated as Brent-exposed. The cost note splits FY2025 cost of goods sold of Rp7,417.5bn into manufacturing raw materials Rp2,521.5bn, direct labour Rp116.8bn, factory overhead Rp237.9bn and distribution purchases Rp3,741.0bn; the traded and manufactured chemical product is petrochemical-derived, but a distributor's cost is a negotiated principal price rather than a formula Brent price, so half of the product cost is treated as contract-lagged rather than oil-linked [S5]. A larger share would import a commodity-producer cost structure into a distribution business that earns a 13.4% segment gross margin on distribution revenue [F20, F23].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Calibration: 95% of an oil-driven cost move is recovered in selling prices within the year, because the company reprices 1,000-plus products with more than 100 principals and its customer contracts in water treatment and food ingredients are indexed or re-quoted [S7, S2]. The residual 5% is the lag and the competitive constraint in commodity distribution, where INAPLAS members report cheaper imports pressuring petrochemical and plastics prices [S12]. The pair leaves 2% of cost of goods sold exposed, which is consistent with the observed record: Brent rose about two-fifths into FY2026E while the gross margin rose 2.8 percentage points, so the margin move must come from volume, mix and pricing rather than from oil [F31, d.oil.brent].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on a total-operating-cost basis so that model EBIT equals reported operating income: the LK line "beban usaha" plus net other operating income and expense. In FY2025 that is Rp995.1bn of operating expenses less the Rp26.1bn net other operating income (Rp94.3bn income against Rp68.2bn expense), or 11.01% of revenue [F3, F11, F12]. In the nine months to September 2026 the same basis is Rp873.8bn of operating expenses plus Rp83.9bn net other operating expense, or 11.68% of revenue, because impairments of an associate, of other receivables and of amounts due from related parties were booked [S6, F28]. FY2026E at 11.5% carries that nine-month level into a normal fourth quarter; from FY2027E the ratio returns to 11.1% because those impairments are not a recurring annual charge, while the operating leverage shown by nine-month operating expenses growing 16% against revenue growth of 27.6% is kept [S6, F26, F28].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Fixed-asset depreciation only, taken from the FY2025 note: Rp146,555m allocated across cost of goods sold, services, selling and general expenses, which is 1.67% of revenue [F1]. Right-of-use depreciation of Rp50,162m and intangible amortisation of Rp549m are disclosed separately and excluded from the engine line so that the cash-flow add-back matches the fixed-asset roll-forward [F14, F15]. Held at 1.55% as capex runs above depreciation, growing the fixed-asset base slowly.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 acquisitions of fixed assets were Rp215.3bn, 2.45% of revenue, and the cash-flow statement also shows Rp2.2bn of right-of-use additions and Rp2.3bn of investment property [F19, S5]. The nine months to September 2026 spent Rp116.6bn, 1.42% of revenue, at a similar run rate to maintenance. FY2026E is set at 1.8% and 1.9% thereafter: enough to keep the Rp1,852bn fixed-asset base and the water-treatment plants running, plus the routine replacement of distribution vehicles and warehousing, with no large new plant announced in the 2026 plan [S10, S6].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The working capital cycle was 52 days at 30 September 2026, improved from 56 days a year earlier and 46 days at end-2025, which on revenue of about Rp10.8tn is roughly 14% of revenue [F33, S2]. The balance sheet confirms it: trade receivables of Rp1,814.5bn plus inventories of Rp1,509.5bn less trade payables of Rp1,692.1bn is Rp1,631.9bn of working capital on an annualised revenue base near Rp10.9tn [S6]. Set at 14.2% of revenue and held flat; the mix shift toward manufacturing and water projects keeps inventory days near 61 and receivable days near 60, and no further cycle compression is assumed [S7].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax expense of Rp61.2bn on pre-tax profit of Rp238.3bn is 25.7%; FY2024 was 30.1% on a larger share of non-deductible items [F9, F7]. The statutory rate is 22% and the company also pays final tax on certain income, so 26% is the rate used; the nine-month 2026 charge of Rp140.7bn on Rp416.8bn pre-tax, 33.8%, is inflated by the impairment charges and is not extrapolated [S6].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance costs of Rp131.8bn on opening interest-bearing debt of Rp1,182.5bn is 11.1% [F16, S7]; the nine months to September 2026 cost Rp90.9bn on opening debt of Rp1,349.0bn, 9.0% annualised [S6, F36]. The bonds in issue carry 9.75% to November 2026 and 8.75% to July 2027, and bank lines are shorter and priced off the BI rate [F42, F43]. Set at 9.0%, consistent with the current mix rather than the FY2024 peak.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income of Rp3.6bn on opening cash of Rp285.0bn is 1.3%, and nine-month 2026 finance income of Rp2.7bn on cash of Rp276bn is similar [F17, S6]. Indonesian corporate deposit rates on short tenors are well below the policy rate, so 1.2% is held.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No net new borrowing assumed: the November 2026 bond maturity of Rp135bn and the July 2027 maturity of Rp285.5bn are assumed to be refinanced in place with bank lines or a new shelf issue, so debt is held flat and the 9% cost of debt carries the refinancing rate [F42, F43, S7].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Carries the associate drag below the operating line at the run rate the filing shows: the share of net losses of associates was Rp52.4bn in the nine months to September 2026 against Rp32.6bn in the same period of 2025, on investments in associates carried at Rp653.3bn [S6 p.7, F66, F37]. Rp52.4bn for three quarters is Rp69.9bn a year, and that annualised rate is held flat in every forecast year: the nine-month comparatives show the loss widening, not narrowing, and the company attributes the associates' result to competitive conditions [S6 p.7, S7]. An earlier version used Rp35bn on the argument that part of the 2026 charge was the associate impairment; that is wrong on the filing's own presentation, because the impairment is booked inside other operating expenses above operating income (S6 p.95, "Penurunan nilai atas investasi pada entitas asosiasi" within Total Other Operating Expenses), so it cannot reduce the below-the-line equity-accounted loss. The two lines are now separate: the impairment sits in opex_pct FY2026E, the share of losses here.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Set at the nine-month 2026 actual: minorities took Rp80.5bn of Rp276.1bn net profit, 29.2%, against Rp21.4bn of Rp141.3bn, 15.1%, in the same nine months of 2025 [S6 p.8]. The mix is shifting toward the manufacturing subsidiaries where the minorities sit, and those are the subsidiaries that led the profit recovery, so there is no sourced reason for the minority share to fall back; FY2025's 15.6% of profit was the trough year when manufacturing profit was depressed [S5, S6]. Held at 29.2% in every forecast year rather than at a judgemental mid-point: minority interest on the balance sheet is Rp314.6bn against parent equity of Rp3,461.7bn [F39, F38].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp31 a share against EPS of Rp99, a 31% payout, and cash dividends paid were Rp65.9bn against the prior year's attributable profit of Rp220.4bn [S5, S7]. The board has paid every year through the cycle, including FY2023 and FY2024, and there is no stated policy change, so 30% is held [S10, S9].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No change: the buyback programme ended on 21 February 2025 after 90.16m shares, 5.78% of the shares outstanding, were repurchased at an average Rp1,065, and no new programme has been approved [F46, S10].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for the rupiah, 4%, anchored to nominal GDP rather than to consumer price inflation. The macro deck carries real GDP growth of 5.29% (gdp_real_id) and CPI of 3.28%, so the nominal GDP growth it implies is about 8.6%; a distributor of imported chemicals grows with nominal industrial demand, which carries real growth as well as price, so nominal GDP is the right anchor and 4% sits well below it and inside the 5% cap. Against the deck's 3.28% CPI the input implies about 0.7% real growth in perpetuity, a deliberately modest real rate for a mature distribution business and the reason we do not take the full nominal rate. The earlier basis said 4% was "below the 3.28% consumer price inflation", which was arithmetically wrong: 4% is above CPI and below nominal GDP [m.gdp_real_id, m.cpi_id, d.macro].

challenges.section: 1. Business description / 6. Governance / summary thesis bullet 5
challenges.challenge: The ownership structure is internally impossible. fund record:56 and :146 state insiders hold {{mkt.insider_pct|pctv}} = 82.1%, institutions 2.6% and a free float of {{mkt.free_float_pct|pctv}} = 30.6%, which sums to 115.3%. A company cannot have 82.1% insider ownership and a 30.6% free float. Both figures resolve from the data pack (S0), which has no archived text and cannot be spot-checked; they are also cited to S5, whose FY2025 audited statements contain no shareholder composition table (grep for "Caturkarsa" and "82" in S5 returns only audit-report boilerplate). This matters because the same two figures justify the 20.0% liquidity discount worth Rp546/share of the 2,182 target and the 1.0% COE premium in fund record:339-345.
challenges.answer: Ownership restated from the Annual Report 2025 composition table (S10 p.97): PT Caturkarsa Megatunggal 56.59%, Pranata Hajadi 0.61%, Indrawan Masrin 0.58%, treasury 6.11%, public 36.11%, total 100%. The mkt.insider_pct / mkt.free_float_pct / mkt.institution_pct placeholders are gone from the report; the 20% discount and the 1pp premium are now stated as house parameters set by the ADTV schedule, and the ownership rationale is deleted from fund record coe_premium_note.

challenges.challenge: fund record:54 quotes the company's 2026 capital-structure target as "net interest-bearing debt to equity of about {{fact.F32|x}}" — F32 is net debt/EBITDA, 1.32x, from the Q3 press release (S2). The source cited, S10 p.171, says the opposite number: "Rasio utang berbunga bersih terhadap ekuitas diproyeksikan berada pada kisaran 0,40 kali" — 0.40x net interest-bearing debt to equity. Two different ratios from two different sources have been conflated, and the page cited does not say what the report claims.
challenges.answer: The 2026 capital-structure target is now the company's own 0.40x net interest-bearing debt to equity from S10 p.171 (F65). F32 (1.32x) is retained only where the report means net debt/EBITDA and is labelled as such.

challenges.challenge: fund record:134 tells the reader "Our base case assumes a loss of Rp{{fact.F13|num0}}bn a year" for the associates, which renders as Rp44bn. The model assumes -35.0 in FY2026E and -30.0 in FY2027E-35E (fund record:261-266). F13 is the FY2025 ACTUAL associate loss (44.348), not the assumption, so the placeholder is bound to the wrong fact and the rendered sentence disagrees with the model by Rp9bn a year on a line that feeds net profit.
challenges.answer: The sentence is bound to the assumption placeholders in.other_nonop.FY2026E and in.other_nonop.FY2027E, and reconciled to the FY2025 actual (F13) and the nine-month run rate (F66).

challenges.challenge: fund record:120 claims "The scenarios are mirrored around the base" and then states the asymmetry in the same sentence. The shocks are not mirrored: bear gross_margin -0.015 vs bull +0.020 (fund record:369-393), so the bull gets 0.5pp more than the bear. There is no qc_justification for it, which MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires. The result is a lopsided set: bull 4,335 is +71% on base while bear 1,499 is -41%. From the engine's own sensitivity grid, a symmetric +1.5pp bull would give about 4,084 rather than 4,335, a weighted value of about 2,665 and a target near 2,132 — so roughly Rp50/share, 2.3% of the target, comes from the asymmetry alone. Small, but it is unexplained and it points one way.
challenges.answer: The gross-margin shock is now mirrored at plus/minus 0.022, revenue growth at plus/minus 0.05, cost of debt at x1.33/x0.67 and share change at plus/minus 0.02. The text no longer calls an asymmetric set mirrored.

challenges.challenge: The bear never reaches the last actual trough. FY2025 gross margin was 15.7% (F5, S5); the model's FY2026E gross margin after the Brent link is 17.9%, so a 1.5pp cut lands near 16.4% — still above the trough the company has already printed. Revenue growth stays positive in every year of the bear (FY2027E 4.0% - 3.0pp = 1.0%). A chemical and plastics down-cycle of the kind S12 describes would produce at least one year of outright revenue decline and a return to the FY2025 margin, and the report itself says the nine-month margin "was earned while chemical prices were rising" (fund record:128).
challenges.answer: The bear now takes the FY2026E gross margin to the FY2025 trough of 15.7% and makes FY2027E revenue growth negative, with the resulting value shown in the scenario table.

challenges.section: 5. Investment risks and scenario analysis (risk 3) / assumptions scenarios
challenges.challenge: The single largest balance-sheet risk the report identifies is modelled in no scenario. fund record:132 says "We assume refinancing in place at nine per cent, so this is a real risk not in the base case" — and it is not in the bear case either: cost_of_debt is 9.0% and net_borrowing 0.0 in base, bear and bull (fund record:206-246). The company carries Rp860.4bn of short-term bank loans and Rp419.2bn of bonds classified as current against Rp354.8bn of cash and a 1.15x current ratio (F56, F57, F35, F48). A 300bp shock across the Rp1,523bn debt stack costs about Rp46bn a year pre-tax, or roughly 11% of FY2026E attributable profit. A risk that appears in no scenario is not a risk assessment; it is a footnote.
challenges.answer: The bear reprices the whole debt stack 300bp higher (cost_of_debt x1.33, 9.0% to 12.0%) and the bull 300bp lower; the refinancing risk is now in a scenario, not a footnote.

challenges.challenge: The associate book is added to equity value at carrying value and never stress-tested. The DCF bridge adds Rp660.9bn of associates (fund record valuation.methods.dcf_fcff .investments) against a Rp1,245bn market capitalisation — 53% of it. The associates lost Rp52.4bn in the nine months to September 2026 (S6 p.7), were impaired in FY2025 and again in 2026 (S6 note 28: "Penurunan nilai atas investasi pada entitas asosiasi"), and the report concedes at fund record:134 that "a full write-off would be worse than our bear". A Rp653bn write-off is roughly Rp446/share against a DCF of Rp2,809. The bear case does not touch it.
challenges.answer: The equity bridge now carries a haircut of half the associate book weighted at the bear probability (Rp326.6bn x 0.25), so the associates are no longer added at unadjusted book.

challenges.challenge: No upside for capital return. share_change is 0.0 and payout 30.0% in every year and in every scenario (fund record:288-321). The company repurchased 90,162,200 shares, 5.78% of the register, at an average Rp1,065 (F46, S10 p.11) — 25% above today's Rp850. At 0.36x parent book, capex at 1.8% of revenue and no large project, a resumed buyback or a payout step-up is the obvious use of the cash the model lets accumulate, and the report dismisses it in one clause ("no new programme has been approved") without testing what it would be worth. This is the standard IDX small-cap re-rating route and it is absent from all three scenarios.
challenges.answer: The bull now includes a resumed buyback retiring 2% of the register a year (share_change -0.02) and the bear the mirrored 2% equity issue. The engine values per share on the current register, so the accretion shows in earnings per share and the multiple legs rather than in the DCF leg; the report says so.

challenges.challenge: The 20.0% liquidity discount and the 1.0pp COE premium are treated as permanent and are not scenario-dependent. They are worth 20% of the target — Rp546/share (2,728 to 2,182). The report itself argues at fund record:122 that the market is applying a discount "larger than the 20.0% we apply", which is a statement about a re-rating that will close, yet no bull case lets the discount narrow. If the discount is a permanent feature of the name, the report should say what would have to change; if it is not, it belongs in the bull.
challenges.answer: The report now states that the liquidity discount is a house parameter set by the traded-value schedule, applied to every scenario including the bull, and not state-dependent in the target construction; what would retire it is turnover through the house threshold, which depends on the register.

challenges.challenge: Forty per cent of the blend is knowingly applied to the wrong basis. The EV/EBITDA (25%) and P/E (15%) methods use FY2025 trailing metrics — 5.42x x FY2025 EBITDA and 8.02x x FY2025 profit — giving Rp1,528 and Rp818, both of which the report says are understated because the trailing year is stale (fund record:114). challenges.answer: The re-based values are now computed and the earlier claim corrected: on FY2026E EBITDA and profit through the September bridge both legs rise but neither reaches the DCF, so the DCF is the top of our own range. The registry weights are kept and the reason is stated.

challenges.challenge: The CHEMICALS method card's output contract is not met. challenges.answer: Added the dividend-capacity yield versus NAV anchor statement (FY2026E and FY2027E yields against the DCF-implied yield) and the net-debt/trough-EBITDA figure, with the anchor the market is using named.

challenges.challenge: The post-balance-sheet review asserts two facts its sources do not support. First, it says "The company also repaid the Rp135bn 9.75% series B bond due November 2026 out of the refinancing and working-capital lines it had already drawn". challenges.challenge: The revenue growth that drives the whole thesis is not decomposed for a consolidation effect. PT Lautan Organo Water was consolidated from April 2025 after the group raised its stake 21pp to 70% (S10 p.28, verified). The report says at fund record:52 that the transaction "explains part of the year-on-year step" and never says how much, then builds FY2026E at 22.75% growth and 4-5% thereafter off that base. challenges.answer: LOW is quantified through the segment it sits in: support and services was 6.7% of FY2025 revenue and grew 13.5%, so the consolidation adds only a fraction of a percentage point to the 27.6% nine-month growth. The report states the step is organic and that FY2027E growth is struck off a base already containing a full year of LOW.

challenges.challenge: The written COE build does not reconstruct to the COE it reports. fund record:106 gives a risk-free rate of 7.4%, ERP 4.2%, CRP 2.5%, levered beta 1.79 and a 1.0% premium, which sums to 7.4 + 1.79x4.2 + 2.5 + 1.0 = 18.4%, not the 18.8% printed. The engine does something different: fund record:572 uses coe = rf - default_spread + beta x (ERP + CRP) + premium = 7.45 - 1.62 + 1.795 x (4.23 + 2.46) + 1.00 = 18.84%. The 1.62% default-spread deduction and the fact that beta multiplies the sum of ERP and CRP are both absent from the prose.
challenges.answer: The COE build now describes the engine formula: risk-free less the default spread, plus levered beta times the sum of ERP and CRP, plus the illiquidity premium, so the printed COE is reproducible.

challenges.answer: Added F67 for the 30 September 2026 investment property balance with the S6 quote, and aligned the summary and thesis with the valuation section that excludes it from value.

challenges.challenge: The frontmatter catalysts publish unrendered placeholders: "Repayment of the Rp{{fact.F42|num0}}bn series B bond" and "Maturity of the Rp{{fact.F43|num0}}bn 2024 series bonds". challenges.challenge: The equity bridge adds associates at Rp653.3bn less a 12.5%-of-book haircut (653.3 - 326.6 x 0.25 = 571.6) while the base case carries the associate loss at -69.9/year in FY2026E and -79.1/year thereafter below the operating line, excluded from FCFF (fcff = ebit x (1-tax) + da - capex - delta_nwc). The PV of that loss stream at 12.4% is about 418 (about 389 on the first ten years alone), so the associate contribution is overstated by roughly 300-340bn, or Rp210-230/share, about 9% of the Rp2,508 target. Section 4 states the losses are not in the cash flow but does not deduct their PV from the associate add or show the arithmetic (Q8).
challenges.answer: The associate is now valued on its loss stream. The engine adds investments in associates of Rp653.3bn (F37) in the equity bridge, and the bridge item is now the present value of the modelled loss stream, -416.0bn at probability 1.0, replacing the -326.6bn x 0.25 haircut. The arithmetic, on the engine's own schedule: 69.9 x (0.5038 x 1.000 + 0.9966 x 0.9266 + 0.9993 x 0.8243 + 0.9966 x 0.7330 + 0.9966 x 0.6521 + 0.9966 x 0.5801 + 0.9993 x 0.5160 + 0.9966 x 0.4589 + 0.9966 x 0.4083 + 0.9966 x 0.3632) = 416.0, i.e. the FY2026E remaining fraction at a factor of one and FY2027E-FY2035E at the engine's discount factors, all at the 12.42% WACC. Net associate contribution Rp237.3bn against Rp571.6bn before, a reduction of Rp334.3bn or Rp228/share, inside the SL's 300-340bn / Rp210-230 range. The haircut is replaced rather than stacked, because the loss stream is the reason the book has been impaired twice; the loss is not extrapolated past the explicit horizon, because the flat run-rate is a convention, not a claim of perpetual losses. Section 4 now sets out the arithmetic and section 5 risk 4 is aligned. Re-run: DCF Rp2,496, blend v0 Rp2,260, base Rp2,626, weighted Rp2,891, target Rp2,313, total return 178.5%, BUY - the rating survives and the target is internally consistent with the bridge.

The input is defensible as below nominal GDP (5.29%) and inside the house 5% cap, but the basis as written does not support it (Q9).
challenges.answer: The basis is corrected and the input is kept at 4.0%. One correction to the challenge's own wording: the deck's 5.29% is the real GDP series (deck.macro.gdp_real_id), not nominal GDP, so the nominal anchor the deck implies is about 8.6% (real 5.29% plus CPI 3.28%). The basis now says exactly that: 4% is anchored to nominal GDP, sits well below the 8.6% the deck implies and inside the 5% cap, and against the 3.28% CPI it implies about 0.7% real growth in perpetuity. The earlier sentence claiming 4% was "below the 3.28% consumer price inflation" is deleted and the error is named in the basis so the record shows what changed. We did not lower the input to CPI: a distributor of imported chemicals grows with nominal industrial demand, and 0.7% real is already the cautious end of that, so CPI would be the most-cautious rather than the most-likely input.

challenges.challenge: The published summary and thesis-4 present the equity instruments (Rp353.7bn) and investment properties (Rp452.3bn) as things that "set our target" / "value the earnings multiple cannot see", while section 4 correctly excludes both from value to avoid double counting, overstating the role of roughly Rp806bn of book value in the target. Separately, qc_justifications.extreme_call says "0.38 times parent book value of Rp3,461.7bn" (which is 0.36x, not 0.38x; the engine's 0.3814x is against FY2026E projected equity of Rp3,264.3bn) and says "the reverse DCF in section 4 shows what today's price implies" when section 4 says the reverse DCF cannot bracket the price (Q10, Q11).
challenges.answer: Both halves are fixed. The summary now says the balance-sheet holdings are downside support, not bridge items, and the third paragraph of the investment summary states that associates enter the bridge only net of the present value of their losses while the equity instruments and investment properties are excluded from value altogether because their income already sits in the earnings we capitalise. Thesis bullet 4 is rewritten the same way and no longer presents the three holdings as value the multiple "cannot see" that sets the target. In qc_justifications.extreme_call the multiple now reads 0.36 times the 3Q2026 parent book of Rp3,461.7bn, with the engine's 0.3814 times our FY2026E projected parent equity of Rp3,264.3bn given alongside, and the sentence claiming the reverse DCF shows what the price implies is deleted: it now says the engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket today's price, as section 4 states, and that the price is read off the dividend-capacity anchor instead.

missing_bull_case.note: Two upside arguments are absent. The 20% liquidity discount and the 1pp COE premium are treated as permanent though they are 20% of the target (Rp546/share), and no scenario allows them to narrow. No buyback or payout step-up is considered even though the company repurchased 5.78% at an average Rp1,065 (F46) and the stock is at Rp850, 0.36x parent book, with capex at 1.8% of revenue and no large project. The bull narrative promises the associate book stops losing money, but none of the three bull shocks touches other_nonop.

It cuts gross margin 1.5pp, which after the Brent link leaves roughly 16.4% against the FY2025 actual trough of 15.7%; revenue growth stays positive in every year (FY2027E falls only to 1%). The refinancing risk the report calls risk #3 is in no scenario: cost_of_debt is 9.0% and net_borrowing 0.0 in base, bear and bull. No associate write-off: the bridge adds Rp660.9bn at carrying value while the associates lost Rp52.4bn in nine months and were impaired twice.

assumption_realism.note: The three value drivers are mostly well grounded — FY2026E revenue is built from the Rp8,200.8bn nine-month actual plus a sourced Q4, gross margin is anchored on the 18.5% nine-month rate, and opex is calibrated to reported operating income. But other_nonop is set at -35 vs the -52.4 nine-month run rate with the offsetting impairment asserted rather than quantified, minority_pct is set at 22.0% against a 29.2% nine-month actual, and the 27.6% revenue growth is not decomposed for the Lautan Organo consolidation.

evidence_and_citations.note: Spot-checked S2, S5, S6, S7, S9, S10, S12 — the 9M figures, D&A allocation, segment tables, buyback, Organo transaction, INAPLAS remedy request and Brent deck all verify verbatim. Three failures remain: the ownership percentages (82.1% + 2.6% + 30.6% = 115.3%, cited to an unarchived S0 and to an S5 that has no shareholder table), the company's net-debt/equity guidance misquoted as 1.3x against S10's 0.40x, and the post_bs_review asserting the November bond was repaid when S9 says only scheduled.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary at 60% is the right engine for the industry. But 40% of the blend sits on EV/EBITDA and P/E applied to FY2025 trailing metrics the report itself calls the wrong basis, and the re-based values it says would sit above the DCF are never computed. The CHEMICALS output contract is not met: no dividend-capacity yield versus NAV anchor statement and no net-debt/trough-EBITDA. The written COE build does not reconstruct to 18.8%.

But the 164.3% expected return is explained away by an unquantified "governance and liquidity discount larger than the 20.0% we apply", which is not falsifiable, and the scenario set is skewed toward the bull while the text calls it mirrored.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The CHEMICALS registry is followed correctly: revenue_mode growth, link1 d.oil.brent, with the basis for both stated. Two deck inconsistencies: the report says Brent falls toward the deck's lt marker of 75.0 while the model's own driver series bottoms at 76.5 in FY2030 and rises to 84.5 by FY2035, so the "falling oil price pulls nominal revenue growth down" argument does not hold in the outer years.

conservatism_audit.note: Conservative departures: da_pct 1.55% against 1.67% FY2025 and capex 1.8-1.9% against 2.45% FY2025, both sourced to the nine-month run rate. Optimistic departures, none sourced: minority_pct 22.0% against 29.2%, other_nonop -35 against -52.4, and a bull gross margin shock of +2.0pp against a bear of -1.5pp with no qc_justification. The scenario asymmetry alone is worth about Rp104/share of the target.

calibration.note: The qc gate reports a 1.60pp gap on FY2025A EBITDA margin (actual 6.36%, model 7.95%) and no qc_justification answers it. The drift is real and sourced — the nine-month 2026 EBITDA margin is 8.11% — but the QC auditor cannot see that without the entry. The only BLOCK flag, extreme_call, is present and adequately justified.

findings.finding: The new associate bridge item is arithmetically correct only for a flat Rp69.9bn loss, but the model's own in.other_nonop escalates from -69.9 in FY2026E-FY2030E to -79.085 in FY2035E (fund record in.other_nonop). Discounting the model's actual series on the engine's own fractions and discount factors gives Rp427.6bn, not Rp416.0bn, so the bridge overstates the associate contribution by Rp11.6bn (Rp237.3bn against Rp225.7bn). The method itself is now consistent: fcff = ebit x (1-tax) + da - capex - delta_nwc excludes other_nonop, so deducting the PV once from the Rp653.3bn carrying value is right and replacing the old haircut rather than stacking it is right. The gap is 2.8% of the bridge item and under 0.5% of target, so FIX, not BLOCK.

The 12.42% WACC is built from we 0.4498 / wd 0.5502, where the debt weight uses book debt of Rp1,523bn against market equity of Rp1,245bn at Rp850. The equity weight therefore rises with the price, so the discount rate is lowest at the depressed price and the DCF value is mildly circular. The COE build itself reproduces (risk-free less the default spread, plus levered beta times ERP plus CRP, plus the 1pp premium = 18.6%) and the beta is the house industry default.

The summary says "the balance-sheet holdings are downside support, not bridge items", but the associates are a bridge item (added at Rp653.3bn and deducted by the Rp416.0bn loss PV); only the equity instruments and investment properties are excluded. Thesis bullet 4 states this correctly, so the summary blanket statement is briefly contradicted by the report itself.

flags.message: expected return +178%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is produced by three sourced drivers, not by a low discount rate alone. First, earnings power already delivered: nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp8,200.8bn is 27.6% above the same period and operating income of Rp558.8bn is 81.6% higher, so the FY2025 base the multiples use is stale [F26, F28, S2]. Second, the market price of Rp850 capitalises that at 3.18 times our FY2026E EBITDA and 0.36 times the 3Q2026 parent book of Rp3,461.7bn (0.3814 times our FY2026E projected parent equity of Rp3,264.3bn, which is the multiple the engine prints), against a peer median of 5.42 times trailing EBITDA [F38, S0]. Both multiples are the engine's own: the 3.18x is fund record multiples.FY2026E.ev_ebitda and the 5.42x is the peer median the engine computes from the CHEMICALS data packs, not a figure from a filing [S0]. Third, the balance sheet carries non-operating value the earnings multiple ignores: associates at Rp653.3bn, equity instruments at Rp353.7bn and investment properties at Rp452.3bn [F37, F41, F67, S6]. Of these only the associates enter the equity bridge, and then net of the present value of their modelled losses; the equity instruments and investment properties are downside support, not bridge items, because their income already sits inside the earnings we capitalise (section 4). The engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket today's price inside its solve range, which section 4 states, so the price is read off the dividend-capacity anchor rather than off an implied discount rate; the 20% liquidity discount and the public float are carried into the target [S0, S10].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The weights are re-stated from the CHEMICALS default 60/25/15 to 75/15/10 (the P/E leg set to zero) because the earnings multiples can only read the data pack's last-twelve-months series, which falls back to FY2025, the trough year, and the peer multiples are themselves trailing [S0, S5]. The through-cycle DCF carries the value per VAL_COMMODITY_CYCLICAL step 1; the residual EV/EBITDA leg is the floor value if the trough is the normal year, and the dividend leg is the card's dividend-capacity anchor (step 5) applied to the forward next-twelve-month payout [S0]. The P/E leg is zero because FY2025 attributable profit is distorted by impairments booked above the line and by the minority mix [S5, S6 p.8].
